Local Tastes
Vada Pav
Mumbai's defining street food — a spiced potato fritter in a soft bread roll with three chutneys. Every street corner has a stall; the best are outside railway stations.
Dadar Station forecourt · Dadar
Pav Bhaji
A thick, butter-rich vegetable curry served with soft bread rolls griddled in more butter — invented in the 1850s as a quick meal for textile mill workers.
Sardar Refreshments · Tardeo
Bhel Puri
Puffed rice tossed at speed with sev, chopped onion, potato, coriander, tamarind and green chutney — assembled in seconds and eaten immediately.
Chowpatty Beach · Chowpatty
Bombay Sandwich
White bread, a specific layer of boiled potato, cucumber, tomato, beetroot and green chutney, toasted or not — the version that exists nowhere else.
Cannon Pav · near CST · Fort
Falooda
A cold layered dessert drink — rose syrup, basil seeds, vermicelli noodles, milk and ice cream — sold at dedicated falooda shops in Mohammed Ali Road and Bhendi Bazaar.
Badshah Cold Drink House · Mohammed Ali Road
Food Delivery
Zomato
Foreign number: accepted. — verification SMS reaches international numbers with a short delay; WhatsApp OTP available as backup.
Mumbai's dominant food delivery app, covering every neighbourhood from Colaba to Bandra and the suburbs; enormous restaurant pool from street food to fine dining. Delivery times are fast and tracking reliable.
zomato.com
Swiggy
Foreign number: accepted. — OTP arrives via SMS; WhatsApp OTP offered as a fallback if SMS fails.
Zomato's main competitor, equally well stocked in Mumbai — similar restaurant selection, comparable prices. Swiggy Instamart adds 30-minute grocery delivery. Response times on a par with Zomato.
swiggy.com

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted. — SMS verification reaches international numbers without issue; WhatsApp OTP is available as a backup.
The most reliable option for visitors in Mumbai — clean vehicles, upfront pricing, a driver name and plate you can verify before getting in. Covers all zones including South Mumbai and Bandra; surge pricing applies during rush hours and rain.
uber.com
Ola
Foreign number: not accepted — Ola requires an Indian mobile number; sign-up with a foreign number is blocked at the OTP stage. Use Uber instead.
India's largest ride-hailing company, dominant in many cities but effectively inaccessible to visitors without a local SIM. The app is practical once you have an Indian number — the driver pool is large and prices are comparable to Uber.
olacabs.com
Mumbai Metro
Foreign number: not required — Metro smart cards are bought at station counters with cash; no registration or phone number needed.
An expanding rapid transit network covering Andheri, Ghatkopar, BKC, Goregaon and Aarey — useful for navigating the northern suburbs. The older Western and Central suburban railways go further but are very crowded at peak hours. The Metro is the cleaner, faster option for visitors.
mmrcl.com
Auto-Rickshaws
Foreign number: not required — flagged from the street, no app or sign-up needed.
Available only in the northern suburbs — banned south of Mahim, which covers the entire South Mumbai itinerary. Metered and plentiful in Bandra and Andheri. Rapido also offers auto-rickshaw bookings in these areas. Having a destination written in Hindi is useful.
rapido.bike

Day Trips by Train
Lonavala · 1 hr 30 min
A hill station in the Western Ghats at 625 m — waterfalls, viewpoints over the Sahyadri valleys, the Bhushi Dam, the Karla and Bhaja Buddhist cave complexes and the famous chikki sweet-shops.
book at: Omio
Pune · 3 hr 30 min
The cultural heart of Maharashtra — the Aga Khan Palace, Shaniwar Wada fort, the Osho International Meditation Resort and a thriving café and restaurant scene.
book at: Omio
Nashik · 4 hr
Maharashtra's wine capital and one of India's four Kumbh Mela sites — 50+ wineries in the Nashik Valley, the Panchavati ghats on the Godavari and the ancient Trimbakeshwar Shiva temple.
book at: Omio
Michelin Restaurants
No Michelin Guide is published for Mumbai. The Michelin Guide covers India through its Bib Gourmand selections in Delhi and Kolkata but does not yet include the Mumbai restaurant scene.
Worth Knowing

The monsoon reshapes the city — but it doesn't close it

Mumbai's monsoon runs from June to September, peaking in July. Rainfall can be biblical — the city recorded 944 mm in a single day in 2005. The Gateway of India terrace floods, the Elephanta ferry runs reduced schedules, and Haji Ali Dargah closes when the causeway submerges. What it does not do is shut the city down: the colonial-era restaurants are busiest, the NCPA schedule is full, and Marine Drive in the rain is one of the great urban sights. Travel with waterproof sandals and a small fold-up umbrella; a full rain jacket is rarely needed.

Taxi apps and cash — Mumbai runs on both, and you need both. Uber works well for hotel-to-sight journeys, but the moment you are in a crowd at a street market or entering a temple, cash takes over entirely. ATMs are plentiful along Marine Drive and in Fort but sometimes run dry on weekends. Draw ₹5,000–10,000 before day one. Carry small notes: a ₹500 note for a ₹40 vada pav causes genuine inconvenience.

Dressing for temples requires more than covered shoulders — the major Hindu and Sufi shrines, Siddhivinayak, Mahalaxmi, and Haji Ali, ask for footwear removal at the gate, often on warm stone in direct sun. Wearing slip-on shoes rather than laced trainers saves real time. For Haji Ali Dargah specifically, women must cover their heads in the inner sanctum; a scarf carried in a bag is sufficient.

The Gateway of India sells its own ferry tickets to Elephanta through Maharashtra Tourism — buy them at the booth at the waterfront, not from the private touts standing between the booth and the water. The MTDC ticket includes the Maharashtra Tourism guide on the island; private boats cost more and land at the same jetty. Early departures at 9:00am reach the caves before the heat and the school groups arrive.

South Mumbai and the suburbs are not the same city. Below Mahim Creek: leafy streets, 19th-century architecture, walkable distances, expensive restaurants. Above it: the Metro, auto-rickshaws, Bandra's nightlife, the airport. The rule is: use Uber everywhere — an auto-rickshaw cannot take you south of Mahim, and knowing this in advance prevents the argument at the kerbside.
